lead: This unit explains algebraic structures with one operation and the number theory that grows from divisibility. After it, a student can test whether a set is a semigroup, monoid or group, use cosets and Lagrange's theorem, compute GCDs and modular inverses, and solve simultaneous congruences with the Chinese remainder theorem.
about: This unit moves from one-operation algebra to number theory. Chapter 4.1 defines semigroups and monoids by closure, associativity and identity. Chapter 4.2 adds inverses to get groups and subgroups. Chapter 4.3 studies cyclic and permutation groups and proves Cayley's theorem. Chapter 4.4 uses cosets to prove Lagrange's theorem. Chapter 4.5 introduces normal subgroups, quotient groups and homomorphisms. The last two chapters switch to integers: 4.6 covers divisibility, primes, GCD and the Euclidean algorithm; 4.7 covers congruences, modular inverses, the Chinese remainder theorem, and the named theorems of Fermat, Euler and Wilson. The group chapters supply examples for the number-theory chapters, especially Zₙ and congruence classes.

chapters.idea: A semigroup is a set with a closed associative operation; adding an identity element gives a monoid.
chapters.depth: Define binary operation, closure, associativity and identity. Define semigroup, monoid and commutative monoid. Use examples from integers, strings under concatenation, functions under composition, and 2×2 matrices. Some syllabi spell 'semi-group' and call a monoid a semigroup with identity. Include submonoid only as a definition with one example.

figure.title: Monoid check for powers of 2
figure.aria: A downward flow checks closure, associativity and identity for M={1,2,4,8,...} and shows that 2 has no inverse in M.
figure.caption: The set of powers of 2 is closed under multiplication and has identity 1, but 2 has no inverse inside the set.

chapters.example: Let M = {1,2,4,8,16,…} = {2ⁿ | n ≥ 0} under ordinary multiplication. Show M is a monoid but not a group. Check closure: 2ᵃ·2ᵇ = 2ᵃ⁺ᵇ. The identity is 1 = 2⁰. The inverse of 2 would be 1/2, which is not in M. Hence M is a monoid but not a group.
chapters.trap: Checking only closure and associativity. A monoid also needs an identity. Do not call the positive integers under addition a monoid: 0 is missing.
chapters.prereq: Unit 2 sets and functions; basic number systems.
chapters.leave: Group axioms go to 4.2. Rings and fields are outside this unit.

chapters.idea: A group is a monoid in which every element has an inverse; a subgroup is a nonempty subset that is itself a group under the same operation.
chapters.depth: State group axioms and define order |G|, abelian group, and examples (Z,+), (Q,+), (Q\{0},×), Zₙ under addition modulo n, and symmetry groups. Define subgroup, trivial subgroup, improper subgroup, and give the one-step and two-step subgroup tests. Show that the intersection of subgroups is a subgroup. Some syllabi write 'sub-group'.

figure.aria: The group G=Z8 under addition contains the subset H={0,4}, which is closed and contains inverses.
figure.caption: H={0,4} sits inside G=Z8; adding 4 to 4 gives 0, so 4 is its own inverse.

chapters.example: For G = Z₈ under addition modulo 8, show H = {0,4} is a subgroup. List all subgroups of G. Closure: 4+4 ≡ 0. Identity: 0 ∈ H. Inverse: −0 = 0 and −4 ≡ 4. The subgroups are {0}, {0,4}, {0,2,4,6} and Z₈.
chapters.trap: Checking closure but forgetting the identity or inverse. A subgroup must contain the identity, and the inverse must also lie in the subset.
chapters.leave: Cyclic groups to 4.3; cosets to 4.4; normal subgroups to 4.5.

chapters.idea: A cyclic group is generated by one element; Cayley's theorem says every group is isomorphic to a permutation group.
chapters.depth: Define order of an element, generator, and cyclic subgroup ⟨a⟩. State that a finite cyclic group is isomorphic to Zₙ and an infinite cyclic group is isomorphic to Z; every subgroup of a cyclic group is cyclic. Introduce Sₙ, cycle notation, transpositions and parity. State and prove Cayley's theorem using left multiplication Lₐ(g)=a·g. Some syllabi state Cayley's theorem as 'every group is isomorphic to a permutation group'.

figure.title: Left multiplication in Z₃
figure.aria: Three rows show how left multiplication by 0, 1 and 2 permutes the elements 0,1,2 of Z3.
figure.caption: Each row is a permutation of 0,1,2; the three rows form a permutation group isomorphic to Z3.

chapters.example: For G = Z₃ = {0,1,2} under addition modulo 3, write L₀, L₁, L₂ as permutations of {0,1,2}. Verify Cayley's theorem. Also find the cyclic subgroup generated by 1. The rows are L₀=(0)(1)(2), L₁=(0 1 2), L₂=(0 2 1). The map a ↦ Lₐ is an injective homomorphism, so G is isomorphic to {L₀,L₁,L₂} ≤ S₃. The subgroup ⟨1⟩ is all of Z₃.
chapters.trap: Confusing the order of a group with the order of an element. Cayley's theorem does not say every group is cyclic; it gives a permutation representation.
chapters.prereq: 4.2 groups and subgroups; Unit 3 permutations; Unit 2 bijections.
chapters.leave: Cosets and Lagrange to 4.4; normal subgroups to 4.5.

chapters.idea: Cosets split a group into equal-sized disjoint blocks; Lagrange's theorem says the order of a subgroup divides the order of the group.
chapters.depth: Define left coset aH and right coset Ha, index [G:H], and prove that cosets partition G. Prove Lagrange's theorem by the bijection h ↦ ah. Give corollaries: the order of an element divides |G|, and a group of prime order is cyclic. Use examples in Z₈ and S₃. State the coset equality test aH=bH iff a⁻¹b ∈ H.

figure.title: Cosets of H = {0,4} in Z₈
figure.aria: Four rows list the four cosets of H={0,4} in Z8, each with two elements.
figure.caption: The four cosets each have two elements and together cover all eight elements of Z8.

chapters.example: In G = Z₈ under addition, let H = {0,4}. List the left cosets of H and verify Lagrange's theorem. The cosets are 0+H={0,4}, 1+H={1,5}, 2+H={2,6}, 3+H={3,7}. There are 4 cosets, |G|=8 and |H|=2, so |G|/|H| = 8/2 = 4.
chapters.trap: Assuming aH = Ha for every subgroup. That holds only for normal subgroups. Also, a coset is not a subgroup unless it contains the identity.
chapters.prereq: 4.2 subgroups; 4.3 cyclic examples; Unit 2 equivalence relations.
chapters.leave: Normal subgroups and quotient groups to 4.5.

chapters.idea: A normal subgroup is stable under conjugation, so its cosets form a quotient group; a homomorphism preserves the group operation.
chapters.depth: Define group homomorphism f(ab)=f(a)f(b), kernel, image, and prove that the kernel is a normal subgroup. Define normal subgroup by gHg⁻¹=H and equivalently aH=Ha. Define quotient group G/H. State and use the first isomorphism theorem G/ker f ≅ im f. Examples: f:Z→Zₙ by reduction mod n, and the sign map Sₙ→{1,−1}. Only a few universities add a first look at rings and fields here; give definitions and the examples Z and Q, then stop.

figure.title: First isomorphism theorem for f(n)=n mod 6
figure.aria: A map f from Z to Z6 has kernel 6Z, and the quotient Z/6Z is isomorphic to the image Z6.
figure.caption: The kernel 6Z collapses to the identity, and the quotient Z/6Z matches the image Z6.

chapters.example: Let f: Z → Z₆ be f(n) = n mod 6. Find ker f and im f. Verify G/ker f ≅ im f. The kernel is 6Z = {…,−6,0,6,12,…}. The image is Z₆. The quotient is Z/6Z, and Z/6Z ≅ Z₆.
chapters.trap: Thinking every subgroup is normal. The kernel is always normal, but an arbitrary subgroup need not be. Also check that f(e)=e′ and f(a⁻¹)=f(a)⁻¹ follow from the homomorphism property.
chapters.prereq: 4.4 cosets and Lagrange; 4.2 groups; Unit 2 functions.
chapters.leave: Deeper isomorphism theorems and ring theory go to later courses. Rings and fields beyond definitions are outside this unit's seven chapters.

chapters.idea: Divisibility orders the integers; primes are their building blocks; the GCD can be computed quickly by the Euclidean algorithm.
chapters.depth: Define a|b and prove basic divisibility properties. Define prime and composite, state the fundamental theorem of arithmetic without proof, and prove the infinitude of primes. State the prime number theorem without proof as π(n) ~ n/ln n, where π(n) counts primes ≤ n. Define gcd and lcm, compute them by prime factorization, and use gcd(a,b)·lcm(a,b)=|ab|. Teach the Euclidean algorithm, extended Euclidean algorithm, and Bezout's theorem without proof. Some syllabi call the repeated-division method the Euclidean algorithm.

figure.title: Euclidean algorithm for gcd(252,105)
figure.aria: Repeated division reduces 252 and 105 to gcd 21, then back substitution writes 21 as −2·252 + 5·105.
figure.caption: The last non-zero remainder is 21, and back substitution gives 21 = (−2)·252 + 5·105.

chapters.example: Use the Euclidean algorithm to find gcd(252,105), then write 21 as a linear combination of 252 and 105. 252 = 2·105 + 42; 105 = 2·42 + 21; 42 = 2·21 + 0. The last non-zero remainder is 21. Back substitute: 21 = 105 − 2·42 = 105 − 2(252 − 2·105) = (−2)·252 + 5·105.
chapters.trap: Stopping at the first remainder instead of the last non-zero remainder. Also watch signs during back substitution and do not call 1 a prime.
chapters.prereq: Basic integer arithmetic; Unit 1 proof by contradiction for the infinitude of primes.
chapters.leave: Modular arithmetic and the Chinese remainder theorem to 4.7. Advanced prime-counting proofs are outside this unit.

chapters.idea: Congruence modulo n turns the integers into finitely many residue classes; the Chinese remainder theorem solves simultaneous congruences when the moduli are coprime.
chapters.depth: Define a ≡ b (mod n), residue classes, Zₙ, and operations on classes. Solve linear congruences ax ≡ b (mod n): solvable iff gcd(a,n)|b, with gcd(a,n) solutions modulo n. Find modular inverses by the extended Euclidean algorithm. State and use the Chinese remainder theorem without proof. State Euler's totient φ(n), Wilson's theorem, Euler's totient theorem and Fermat's little theorem without proof. Use small numerical examples for each.

figure.title: Chinese remainder theorem example
figure.aria: Three congruences modulo 3, 5 and 7 combine to the single congruence x ≡ 23 modulo 105.
figure.caption: The three small congruences have one solution modulo 3·5·7 = 105, namely x = 23.

chapters.example: Solve the system x ≡ 2 (mod 3), x ≡ 3 (mod 5), x ≡ 2 (mod 7). From mod 3 and mod 5, x = 8 + 15t. Put this into mod 7: 8 + 15t ≡ 2, so 1 + t ≡ 2, hence t ≡ 1 (mod 7). Then x = 8 + 15(1 + 7s) = 23 + 105s. The solution is x ≡ 23 (mod 105). Check: 23 mod 3 = 2, 23 mod 5 = 3, 23 mod 7 = 2.
chapters.trap: Using the Chinese remainder theorem when the moduli are not pairwise coprime. Also, ax ≡ b (mod n) has no inverse solution when gcd(a,n) ≠ 1; it may still have solutions if gcd(a,n) divides b.
chapters.prereq: 4.6 GCD and Euclidean algorithm; Unit 2 equivalence relations.
chapters.leave: Proofs of Fermat, Euler and Wilson are left out. RSA and cryptographic applications go to later courses.

links: Add inverses to a monoid to get a group.
A group generated by one element is cyclic; Cayley embeds every group in permutations.
Cyclic examples make cosets and Lagrange easy to see.
Cosets become quotient groups when the subgroup is normal.
Quotient groups Z/nZ are the same as congruence classes modulo n.
The Euclidean algorithm gives modular inverses and supports Chinese remainder calculations.
